title: Assessing the potential of LLM-assisted annotation for corpus-based pragmatics and discourse analysis
abstract: Abstract Certain forms of linguistic annotation, like part of speech and semantic tagging, can be automated with high accuracy. However, manual annotation is still necessary for complex pragmatic and discursive features that lack a direct mapping to lexical forms. This manual process is time-consuming and error-prone, limiting the scalability of function-to-form approaches in corpus linguistics. To address this, our study explores the possibility of using large language models (LLMs) to automate pragma-discursive corpus annotation. We compare GPT-3.5 (the model behind the free-to-use version of ChatGPT), GPT-4 (the model underpinning the precise mode of Bing chatbot), and a human coder in annotating apology components in English based on the local grammar framework. We find that GPT-4 outperformed GPT-3.5, with accuracy approaching that of a human coder. These results suggest that LLMs can be successfully deployed to aid pragma-discursive corpus annotation, making the process more efficient, scalable, and accessible.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This article has attracted strong scholarly uptake: OpenAlex records 64 citations, placing it in the top 1% of works in its field and year. The citing record is concentrated in corpus linguistics and pragmatics venues, indicating that the paper is being used as a reference point for methodologically oriented work on LLM-assisted annotation.

Full narrative

Yu, Li, Su, and Fuoli’s 2024 article addresses a practical bottleneck in corpus-based pragmatics and discourse analysis: the difficulty of annotating complex pragmatic features reliably at scale. Its impact profile shows that this methodological contribution quickly found an audience, with 64 citations and a field-normalized standing in the top 1% for its publication year. The citation pattern is especially notable for appearing across journals and edited volumes closely aligned with corpus linguistics, pragmatics, and natural language processing.

The downstream literature suggests that the article is being used not just as background reading but as a touchstone for new LLM-assisted approaches. It is cited most heavily in corpus-linguistic and pragmatics-oriented venues, and the citing works include studies on automated retrieval of speech acts, corpus pragmatics, and LLM use in text linguistics teaching and analysis. That mix points to methodological influence across both research and pedagogy, with the paper helping frame how researchers think about form-function annotation workflows.

Scite also records 20 citation statements, including supporting mentions, which is consistent with the article’s role as an enabling methodological source rather than a contested claim. In addition, the record shows 64 instances of documented reuse and a linked data resource, indicating stewardship beyond the article itself and suggesting that the work sits within a broader, reusable research workflow. The open repository and dataset signals further strengthen its value for researchers seeking to replicate or extend the approach.

Overall, the evidence portrays a paper with clear and early methodological influence in corpus pragmatics and adjacent NLP work. The record is strongest in scholarly reuse and disciplinary citation, while public attention signals are limited in the sources available here. Even so, the combination of high citation standing, concentrated uptake in relevant venues, and reuse of the accompanying research materials indicates that this article has become a meaningful reference for LLM-assisted annotation research.
